title: Review: Distance and angles
description: Questions on the ideas in this chapter, from one star (a check of the definitions) to four stars (combining several ideas). They come in a random order each time.

questions.question: What does $$d(P, Q) = 0$$ tell you about the points $$P$$ and $$Q$$?
options: They are the same point
Nothing, since a distance can be $$0$$ for any two points
They are on the same line
They are close together but different
questions.explanation: The first rule for distance says $$d(P, Q) \ge 0$$, with $$d(P, Q) = 0$$ exactly when $$P$$ and $$Q$$ are the same point (:ref{#distance-rules}).

questions.question: What does the triangle inequality $$d(P, M) \le d(P, Q) + d(Q, M)$$ say in words?
options: Going by way of $$Q$$ is always longer than going straight there
Going from $$P$$ to $$M$$ by way of $$Q$$ is never shorter than going straight there
The three sides of a triangle are always equal
$$Q$$ always lies between $$P$$ and $$M$$
questions.explanation: A detour through a third point covers at least as much ground as the direct route (:ref{#distance-rules}). It can be equal, when $$Q$$ is on the segment $$PM$$, so \"always longer\" is too strong.

questions.question: How does the guide know that $$d(P, Q) = d(Q, P)$$ for all points?
options: It follows from the Pythagoras theorem
It is checked by measuring with a ruler
It is taken as given, as one of the rules for distance
It proves it from the triangle inequality
questions.explanation: \"The same both ways\" is one of the three rules for distance that the guide takes as given and doesn't prove (:ref{#distance-rules}). Every other fact about distance rests on these.

questions.question: For which points $$Q$$ is $$d(P, M) = d(P, Q) + d(Q, M)$$?
options: Only the midpoint of $$PM$$
Every point in the plane
Exactly the points on the line $$PM$$
Exactly the points on the segment $$PM$$
questions.explanation: The first rule for segments says the equation holds exactly when $$Q$$ lies on the segment $$PM$$ (:ref{#segment-rules}). A point on the line but beyond $$M$$ makes the route through it longer.

questions.question: $$Q$$ lies on the line through $$P$$ and $$M$$, but beyond $$M$$. Which is true?
options: No equation of this kind holds, since $$Q$$ is not between any two of the points
questions.explanation: Of three different points on one line, exactly one lies between the other two (:ref{#segment-rules}). Here $$M$$ is between $$P$$ and $$Q$$, so rule 1 for segments gives $$d(P, Q) = d(P, M) + d(M, Q)$$.

questions.question: What is the difference between the circle and the disc with centre $$P$$ and radius $$r$$?
options: The circle is the points at distance at most $$r$$; the disc is the points at distance exactly $$r$$
The circle is the points at distance exactly $$r$$; the disc is the points at distance at most $$r$$
The disc is the circle with its centre removed
They are two names for the same set of points
questions.explanation: The circle is only the edge, $$d(P, Q) = r$$, and the disc is the edge and everything inside, $$d(P, Q) \le r$$ (:ref{#circle}). So a circle has a length but no area, and a disc has an area.

questions.question: Which of these is a rule about lines that the guide takes as given?
options: Any two lines meet in exactly one point
Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal
Two different points lie on exactly one line
Three points always lie on one line
questions.explanation: \"Two points, one line\" is the first rule for lines (:ref{#line-rules}). Parallel lines never meet, so not every pair of lines meets (:ref{#crossing-lines}), and the rectangle fact is proved (:ref{#rectangle-sides}).

questions.question: Which rule for lines fails on the surface of a globe, where any two great circles cross?
options: Every line has at least two points
A ray has one starting point
Two points lie on exactly one line
Exactly one line through a point is parallel to a given line
questions.explanation: On a globe there is no parallel through a point, since every pair of great circles crosses. Rule 2, one parallel through a point, is the rule that makes flat geometry flat (:ref{#line-rules}).

questions.question: Which of these facts about lines does the guide take as given, without proof?
options: Exactly one line through a point is parallel to a given line
Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel
Two lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other
Two lines that are not parallel meet in exactly one point
questions.explanation: One parallel through a point is rule 2 for lines (:ref{#line-rules}). The other three are proved from the rules by contradiction: :ref{#crossing-lines}, :ref{#parallel-transitive} and :ref{#perpendiculars-parallel}.

questions.question: How are the ray $$PQ$$ and the ray $$QP$$ related?
options: They are both the segment $$PQ$$
They start at different points and run in opposite directions
The ray $$QP$$ is the ray $$PQ$$ with $$P$$ removed
They are the same ray
questions.explanation: The starting point comes first in the name. The ray $$PQ$$ starts at $$P$$ and runs on through $$Q$$, while the ray $$QP$$ starts at $$Q$$ and runs back through $$P$$ (:ref{#ray}).

questions.question: Two lines are both perpendicular to the same line. What follows?
options: They meet at a right angle
Nothing, without measuring
They are parallel
They are perpendicular to each other
questions.explanation: If $$L_1 \perp L_2$$ and $$L_2 \perp L_3$$, then $$L_1 \parallel L_3$$ (:ref{#perpendiculars-parallel}). If the two lines met, there would be two different perpendiculars to the same line through one point, which rule 1 for perpendicular lines rules out.

questions.question: How does the guide show that opposite sides of a rectangle have the same length?
options: It takes it as given in the definition of a rectangle
It uses the Pythagoras theorem on the diagonal
It measures the sides in a figure
Opposite sides are parallel, and the rule that parallel lines are the same distance apart everywhere does the rest
questions.explanation: Opposite sides are both perpendicular to a third side, so they are parallel. The rule for the distance between parallel lines then gives equal lengths (:ref{#parallel-distance}, :ref{#rectangle-sides}).

questions.question: An L shape is cut into rectangles of areas $$10$$ and $$6$$. Why is its area $$16$$, whichever way you cut it?
options: Because the rule that areas add holds for any cut into pieces that don't overlap
Because every cut gives pieces of areas $$10$$ and $$6$$
Because the area of a shape is the sum of its side lengths
Because an L shape is a rectangle
questions.explanation: The rules for area say a rectangle has area $$ab$$ and that a region cut into pieces that don't overlap has the sum of their areas as its area (:ref{#area-rules}). So every cut gives the same total.

questions.question: How many angles do two rays from the same point make?
options: Four
Two
It depends on the rays
One
questions.explanation: The two rays split the plane into two regions, and each region with its two edge rays is an angle (:ref{#angle}). That is why a name for an angle needs a rule for which one it means.

questions.question: In these notes, which of the two angles made by the rays $$PQ$$ and $$PM$$ does $$\angle QPM$$ mean?
options: The one turning anticlockwise from $$PQ$$ to $$PM$$
Either, so the name is ambiguous
The one on one side of the line $$PQ$$, which is never more than a straight angle
Always the larger one
questions.explanation: $$\angle QPM$$ is the angle that lies on one side of the line $$PQ$$, so it is never larger than a straight angle (:ref{#angle-name}). The other one is the reflex angle, named in words.

questions.question: The rays $$PQ$$ and $$PM$$ are the same ray. What are the two angles they make?
options: Two zero angles
A right angle and a reflex angle
Two straight angles
A zero angle and a full angle
questions.explanation: One angle has nothing between its arms, the zero angle, and the other is the whole plane, the full angle (:ref{#special-angles}).

questions.question: What is the sector of a disc cut out by an angle?
options: The part of the disc inside the angle, with the disc centred at the vertex
The part of the disc's circle inside the angle
The triangle made by the two arms and the circle
The part of the disc outside the angle
questions.explanation: The sector is the part of a disc centred at the vertex that lies inside the angle (:ref{#sector}). Its curved edge, the part of the circle inside the angle, is the arc.

questions.question: In the turn picture, what does it mean for an angle to have $$x$$ degrees?
options: It is $$\frac{x}{180}$$ of a full turn
It is $$\frac{x}{360}$$ of a full turn
Its arms are $$x$$ units long
Its sector has area $$x$$
questions.explanation: One full turn is split into $$360$$ equal steps, each one degree, so an angle of $$x^\circ$$ is $$\frac{x}{360}$$ of a full turn (:ref{#degree}).

questions.question: How does the definition of degrees make \"a fraction of a turn\" precise?
options: By counting how many right angles fit inside it
By the distance between the ends of the arms
By the share of a disc centred at the vertex that the angle's sector takes up
By measuring the length of the arms
questions.explanation: An angle has $$x^\circ$$ when its sector is $$\frac{x}{360}$$ of the area of a disc centred at its vertex (:ref{#degree}). After this, the guide argues with the turn picture.

questions.question: The definition of degrees doesn't say how big the disc is. Why doesn't that matter?
options: The definition only works for right angles
Every disc in the guide has radius $$1$$
A bigger disc gives a sector with the same area
It is taken as given that the sector is the same fraction of every disc centred at the vertex
questions.explanation: A bigger disc gives a bigger sector, but the same fraction of the disc. That is rule 2 of :ref{#disc-area}, taken as given in this chapter. The Area and scaling chapter proves it (:ref{#area-and-scaling/sector-scaling}).

questions.question: Why is a full turn split into $$360$$ degrees?
options: Because $$360$$ divides evenly by many small numbers, so common fractions of a turn are whole numbers of degrees
Because it is the area of a disc
Because a circle has $$360$$ points
Because it was proved from the rules for distance
questions.explanation: $$360$$ is a multiple of $$2$$, $$3$$, $$4$$, $$5$$, $$6$$, $$8$$, $$9$$, $$10$$ and $$12$$, so halves, thirds, quarters and more are whole numbers of degrees (:ref{#degree}).

questions.question: What does the proof that a straight angle is $$180^\circ$$ use?
options: That the angles of a triangle add up to $$180^\circ$$
That a line through the centre of a disc cuts it into two equal halves
The Pythagoras theorem
That a right angle is $$90^\circ$$
questions.explanation: The arms of a straight angle form a line through the centre of any disc at the vertex, which halves the disc by rule 3 of :ref{#disc-area}. So $$\frac{x}{360} = \frac{1}{2}$$ and $$x = 180$$ (:ref{#straight-angle}). The triangle fact comes much later, so using it here would be circular.

questions.question: How does the guide show that two angles side by side, sharing an arm, add up?
options: It uses the Pythagoras theorem
It takes it as given
Their sectors make up the sector of the whole angle, and areas add
It measures the angles with a protractor
questions.explanation: Degrees are defined by the share of a disc that an angle's sector takes up (:ref{#degree}). The two smaller sectors make up the bigger one without overlapping, so their areas add, and so do the angles (:ref{#angle-addition}).

questions.question: Why does a sector of $$x^\circ$$ in a disc of radius $$r$$ have area $$\frac{x}{360}\pi r^2$$?
options: Because the arc has length $$x$$
It is taken as given
Because the sector is a triangle with base $$r$$
The sector is $$\frac{x}{360}$$ of the disc by the definition of degrees, and the disc has area $$\pi r^2$$
questions.explanation: The definition of degrees says the sector is $$\frac{x}{360}$$ of the disc's area, and rule 1 for discs gives that area as $$\pi r^2$$ (:ref{#sector-area}).

questions.question: Two right triangles have legs of the same lengths. Which of these does the guide take as given, rather than prove?
options: Their hypotenuses, angles and areas all match
Their hypotenuses satisfy $$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$
Their area is $$\frac{ab}{2}$$
Their angles add up to $$180^\circ$$
questions.explanation: The rules for right triangles take the full match as given (:ref{#right-triangle-rule}). The others are proved from it: :ref{#pythagoras}, :ref{#triangle-angle-sum} and :ref{#right-triangle-area}. The Isometries chapter later proves that the hypotenuses and angles match (:ref{#isometries/right-triangles-congruent}).

questions.question: In a right triangle, what do the two angles other than the right angle add up to?
options: It depends on the lengths of the legs
questions.explanation: They always add up to $$90^\circ$$ (:ref{#right-triangle-angles}). So each is less than $$90^\circ$$, and a right triangle has only one right angle.

questions.question: How does the proof that the two other angles of a right triangle add to $$90^\circ$$ work?
options: It uses the angle sum of a triangle, $$180^\circ$$, and takes away $$90^\circ$$
It uses the Pythagoras theorem
It completes a rectangle; the diagonal makes two matching triangles, so the two angles sit side by side in one right-angled corner
It measures the angles with a protractor
questions.explanation: The rectangle's diagonal splits it into two right triangles with the same legs, so a matching angle moves to the other corner, where the two angles fill a right angle (:ref{#right-triangle-angles}). The angle sum is proved later from this result, so using it would be circular.

questions.question: Why is the area of a right triangle with legs $$a$$ and $$b$$ equal to $$\frac{ab}{2}$$?
options: Because $$\frac{ab}{2}$$ is the average of $$a$$ and $$b$$
Because of the Pythagoras theorem
It is taken as given
It is half of a rectangle with sides $$a$$ and $$b$$, split by a diagonal into two triangles of equal area
questions.explanation: Two copies make an $$a$$ by $$b$$ rectangle of area $$ab$$. The two halves have the same legs, so the same area by the rules for right triangles, and each is $$\frac{ab}{2}$$ (:ref{#right-triangle-area}).

questions.question: In a right triangle with legs $$a$$ and $$b$$ and hypotenuse $$c$$, what does the Pythagoras theorem say?
questions.explanation: The square of the hypotenuse is the sum of the squares of the legs (:ref{#pythagoras}). For legs $$3$$ and $$4$$ the hypotenuse is $$5$$, not $$3 + 4 = 7$$.

questions.question: What is the key idea in the guide's proof of the Pythagoras theorem?
options: Draw the perpendicular bisector of the hypotenuse
Fit four copies of the triangle in a square of side $$a + b$$, and add up the area of the square in two ways
Use the angle sum of a triangle
Measure many right triangles and spot the pattern
questions.explanation: The square has area $$(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$$, and it is also four triangles of area $$\frac{ab}{2}$$ plus a middle square of area $$c^2$$. Comparing gives $$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$ (:ref{#pythagoras}). Checking examples could never prove it.

questions.question: In the proof of the Pythagoras theorem, why is each corner of the middle shape a right angle?
options: Because all four of its sides have length $$c$$
Because it is drawn as a square
Because at each corner it sits between two triangle angles adding to $$90^\circ$$, and the three angles together make a straight angle
Because the big square's corners are right angles
questions.explanation: The two triangle angles add up to $$90^\circ$$ (:ref{#right-triangle-angles}), and with the middle corner they fill a straight angle, $$180^\circ$$ (:ref{#straight-angle}). So the middle corner is $$90^\circ$$. Equal sides alone don't make a square.

questions.question: The diagonal of a square with sides of length $$1$$ has length $$\sqrt{2}$$. What does that tell you?
options: The diagonal is $$1.5$$
The diagonal can't be drawn exactly
The diagonal is twice the side
The diagonal's length can't be written as a fraction
questions.explanation: The diagonal is $$\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}$$ (:ref{#pythagoras}), and no fraction squares to $$2$$ (:ref{#numbers/sqrt-two}). So a length you can draw exactly need not be a fraction.

questions.question: How does the guide find the diagonal through a box?
options: One right triangle on the floor, then a second standing upright on the floor's diagonal
By measuring
Three right triangles, one on each face
By the angle sum of a triangle
questions.explanation: The floor's diagonal comes from one right triangle, and the box diagonal is the hypotenuse of a second one with the floor diagonal and an upright edge as legs. That gives $$\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$$, using :ref{#pythagoras} twice.

questions.question: What is the perpendicular bisector of a segment $$PQ$$?
options: The line through $$P$$ perpendicular to $$PQ$$
The line through the midpoint of $$PQ$$ that is perpendicular to $$PQ$$
The line $$PQ$$ itself
Any line perpendicular to $$PQ$$
questions.explanation: It is the line through the midpoint, perpendicular to $$PQ$$, and there is exactly one such line (:ref{#perpendicular-bisector}).

questions.question: The theorem says $$d(P, M) = d(Q, M)$$ exactly when $$M$$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $$PQ$$. What has to be proved?
options: Neither, since it is taken as given
Only that points the same distance from $$P$$ and $$Q$$ are on the bisector
Both directions: each statement leads to the other
Only that points on the bisector are the same distance from $$P$$ and $$Q$$
questions.explanation: \"Exactly when\" claims both directions (:ref{#basic-proofs/exactly-when}). The proof handles both with a chain of statements, each true exactly when the next is (:ref{#perpendicular-bisector-rule}).

questions.question: Which result does the proof of the perpendicular bisector theorem rely on most?
options: Opposite angles are equal
The area of a sector
The angle sum of a triangle
The Pythagoras theorem, applied to the two right triangles made by the perpendicular from $$M$$
questions.explanation: Dropping a perpendicular from $$M$$ to the line $$PQ$$ gives two right triangles sharing a leg. Pythagoras turns equal distances from $$M$$ into equal distances from the foot $$F$$, which makes $$F$$ the midpoint (:ref{#perpendicular-bisector-rule}).

questions.question: A point $$O$$ on the line $$PQ$$ has $$d(O, P) = d(O, Q)$$. What can you conclude?
options: $$O$$ is the midpoint of $$PQ$$
$$O$$ could be anywhere on the line
$$O$$ is beyond $$Q$$
questions.explanation: If $$O$$ were not between $$P$$ and $$Q$$, one of $$P$$ and $$Q$$ would be between $$O$$ and the other, forcing $$d(P, Q) = 0$$ (:ref{#equidistant-on-line}).

questions.question: Why is the hypotenuse of a right triangle longer than each leg?
options: Because the triangle inequality says $$c > a + b$$
Because it is opposite the largest angle, which is taken as given
It isn't always: a leg can be longer
questions.explanation: Pythagoras gives $$c^2 = a^2 + b^2 > a^2$$, and for positive numbers a larger square means a larger number (:ref{#hypotenuse-longest}).

questions.question: What is the shortest distance from a point $$P$$ to a line $$L$$ that doesn't pass through it?
options: The distance to any point of $$L$$, since they are all equal
There is no shortest distance
The distance to the foot of the perpendicular from $$P$$ to $$L$$
The distance measured along a line parallel to $$L$$
questions.explanation: Any other point $$M$$ of $$L$$ makes a right triangle in which $$PM$$ is the hypotenuse and $$PF$$ is a leg, so $$d(P, M) > d(P, F)$$ (:ref{#shortest-distance}, :ref{#point-line-distance}).

questions.question: Why is there a circle through the three corners of every triangle?
options: Every triangle is half of a rectangle
Any three points lie on a circle with centre at one of them
The angles add up to $$180^\circ$$
The perpendicular bisectors of two sides meet at a point the same distance from all three corners
questions.explanation: The two bisectors can't be parallel, or two sides would lie on one line, so they meet at a point $$O$$. Being on both makes $$O$$ the same distance from all three corners, so a circle centred at $$O$$ passes through them (:ref{#circumcentre}).

questions.question: Why are opposite angles equal where two lines cross?
options: Each one plus the angle between them makes $$180^\circ$$
It is taken as given
Because the two lines are perpendicular
Because of the Pythagoras theorem
questions.explanation: With $$\beta$$ between them, $$\alpha + \beta = 180^\circ$$ and $$\beta + \alpha' = 180^\circ$$ by :ref{#angles-on-line}, so $$\alpha = \alpha'$$ (:ref{#opposite-angles}).

questions.question: What do the three angles of any triangle add up to?
options: It depends on the triangle
questions.explanation: Every triangle's angles add up to $$180^\circ$$ (:ref{#triangle-angle-sum}). So two angles decide the third.

questions.question: How does the guide prove that a triangle's angles add up to $$180^\circ$$?
options: By measuring many triangles
It takes it as given
By dropping a perpendicular from one corner to the line of the opposite side and using the right triangle angle result
By cutting out the corners and laying them side by side
questions.explanation: The perpendicular makes right triangles, whose other two angles add to $$90^\circ$$ (:ref{#right-triangle-angles}). Combining them gives $$180^\circ$$ (:ref{#triangle-angle-sum}). Cutting out corners suggests the fact but doesn't prove it.

questions.question: Why does the angle sum proof need more than one case?
options: Acute and obtuse angles need different definitions
Triangles with equal sides behave differently
Right triangles have a different angle sum
The foot of the perpendicular can be a corner, between the two corners, or outside the side
questions.explanation: In the outside case, the triangle is a large right triangle with a small one cut away, so the angles combine by subtraction instead of addition (:ref{#triangle-angle-sum}). Leaving a case out would leave a hole in the proof.

questions.question: Can a triangle have two obtuse angles?
options: No, two angles of more than $$90^\circ$$ would already add to more than $$180^\circ$$
Yes, in a right triangle
Yes, if the third angle is small enough
Yes, any triangle can
questions.explanation: The three angles add up to exactly $$180^\circ$$ (:ref{#triangle-angle-sum}), so at most one angle can be $$90^\circ$$ or more.

questions.question: A line crosses two parallel lines. Which angles are equal?
options: None, unless the line is perpendicular
Corresponding angles and alternate angles
Only angles at the same crossing
Only the right angles
questions.explanation: Alternate angles (the Z shape) are equal, and corresponding angles are equal (:ref{#parallel-angles}). So all eight angles take at most two values.

questions.question: The perpendicular from the top corner meets the line of the base outside the base. What is the triangle's area?
options: There is no height, so the formula fails
Still $$\frac{1}{2}bh$$, with $$h$$ measured to the line of the base
$$\frac{1}{2}b$$ times the length of a side
questions.explanation: The triangle is a large right triangle with a small one cut away, and the difference still comes to $$\frac{1}{2}bh$$ (:ref{#triangle-area}). The height is measured to the line containing the base (:ref{#height}).
